experiments.reasoning: The experiment investigates the preservation qualities of different substances and their effects on preventing or promoting putrefaction.
experiments.description: A mixture was created with yolk of an egg, fresh and diluted in water. A thread dipped in a piece from this mix was placed into separate phials to observe the rate and extent of putrefaction when exposed to heat near a fire after sealing them off.
experiments.quote: The Thread infected the fresh Yolk; for the Putrefaction was more perceptible in the Phial that contained it, than in the other. But this Experiment was not repeated.
experiments.outcome: Thread accelerated putrefaction of fresh yolk when compared to a control phial with diluted egg alone.

experiments.reasoning: This experiment examines how different substances affect the rate at which meat putsrefies in controlled conditions simulating putrid environments and interactions between animal blood serum and meats. It also touches on digestion issues related to these effects.
experiments.description: Sea salt was used with two ounces of water, preserving fresh beef for over 30 hours at body temperature; the effectiveness varied based on quantity ratio (one grain per two ounces).
experiments.quote: One Drachm of Salt preserves two Drachms of fresh Beef, in two Ounces of Water, above 30 Hours, uncorrupted.
experiments.outcome: Salt at one-to-two ratio demonstrated effective meat preservation for extended periods under specific conditions; smaller quantities had different effects on softening and relaxing the texture of meat rather than preventing putrefaction.

experiments.reasoning: An exploration into how various substances mixed with animal blood can impact its propensity to induce or combat septic conditions.
experiments.description: Fresh beef was combined with vipers and the serum of human blood in separate experiments, while another set used only fresh beef without additional agents. The effects on putrefaction were noted.
experiments.quote: The Flies were tried both with fresh Beef, and with the *Serum* of human Blood; the Vipers only with the former... but neither of them haflened Putrefaction.
experiments.outcome: Viper venom did not promote putrefaction in beef; serum from human blood was less effective than vipers alone at inducing decay.

experiments.reasoning: An investigation into the antiseptic properties of common substances and their comparative effectiveness against putrefaction.
experiments.description: Chalk was observed for its effects when combined with ox'se on in a phial, as well as separately infused meat. The interaction between chalk powder and flesh is noted to be significant.
experiments.quote: Twenty Grains of Crabs-eyes prepared...into another Phial was put nothing but Gall and Water; both being placed in the Furnace, the Putrefaction began much sooner where the Powder was, than in the other.
experiments.outcome: Chalk mixed with gall promoted rapid decay when heated compared to phials containing just water and gall alone.

experiments.reasoning: An exploration of the antiseptic effects of chalk in acidic solutions on meat preservation.
experiments.description: Chalk was infused into a phial with flesh and water alongside barley mucilage, observing any decomposition over time under heat digestion conditions.
experiments.quote: The plain Water swelled the Barley... remained sweet; that with the Powder kept the Grain to its natural Size...
experiments.outcome: Barley retained size and sweetness without mucilage production when mixed with chalk, unlike water alone.

experiments.reasoning: An experiment to determine the antiseptic properties of different types of salt on meat preservation and decomposition rates
experiments.description: Salt from Hartshorn was used in conjunction with flesh inside a phial alongside plain water, noticing any changes over time.
experiments.quote: ...but half a Drachm of Salt does not preserve it above 2 Hours longer.
experiments.outcome: Small amounts of salt had limited preserving effect; larger quantities hastened decay rather than preventing putrefaction. Smaller or zero quantity salts induced softening and further decomposition.

experiments.outcome: Chalk and larger salt amounts had no antiseptic effect but rather softened flesh under conditions that would normally preserve food. This suggests their role is not primarily preventative against putrefaction.

experiments.outcome: Acidic solutions from barley infusions produced more air and could prevent decay by generating acidity, suggesting they were not traditional antiseptics but rather influenced meat digestion.
